name: Ring training / planche progressions

lead: Ring training uses suspended gymnastic rings for push, pull and hold exercises, and the planche is a straight-arm hold with the body horizontal above the hands. Practitioners use them to build the broad, muscular upper body of a gymnast.

The rings are unstable, so the body must control the movement as well as lift it, and progressions move from easier variations toward the full skill by adjusting leverage. Both come from gymnastics and calisthenics; Wikipedia describes the planche as the most advanced of the common calisthenics skills, often reached only after years of training. No published study tests ring or planche training for appearance outcomes.

paras: People hang a pair of rings from a bar or frame and work through ring dips, rows, pushups and leaning hold progressions, building toward holds over months to years. It is usually done alongside other calisthenics or lifting.
Advanced straight-arm static holds load the wrists, elbows and shoulders heavily.

web.title: Electromyographic Comparison of Traditional and Suspension Push-Ups

angle.text: Practitioners use ring dips, levers and planche progressions as a skill-based route to upper-body size and a gymnast look. Unstable rings and leverage-based progressions load the muscles hard, building a broader upper body. No studies of appearance outcomes were found.

lead: Ring training and planche progressions are gymnastics-derived strength work for building a developed upper body: broad shoulders, thick arms and chest, and a taut midsection. Gymnastic rings are two rings hung from a frame by straps, used in men's artistic gymnastics; a standard apparatus has rings with an 18 cm inner diameter hung 300 cm from the attachment point.[1] Elements include strength holds such as the iron cross and Maltese cross, and swing elements such as giant swings.[1] People train on rings and work toward the planche because they want the muscular, V-tapered gymnast physique, which they associate with this kind of training.

The planche is a calisthenics static hold in which the body is held parallel to the floor, supported only by straight arms.[2][3] Wikipedia's calisthenics article describes it as the most advanced of the common skills, often reached only after years of training.[2] Athletes usually build up through a progression from frog stand through tuck, advanced tuck and straddle to the full planche, with the arms locked throughout.[3] The main muscles worked are the anterior deltoid and biceps, supported by abdominals, chest, shoulders, lower back and glutes, with triceps, lats and serratus anterior also involved.[3]

Because rings move freely, the body must stabilise them, and an electromyography study of 21 adults found suspension push-ups produced higher activity in the pectoralis major, anterior deltoid and triceps than floor push-ups.[4] On looksmax.org, members describe ring workouts as engaging every muscle fibre and being better for shoulder and elbow health.[5]

paras: Rings are one of the apparatus in men's artistic gymnastics. Judges apply deductions for bent arms in most elements and for using the straps or cables for support or balance [1]. A routine must include elements from groups covering swings, strength holds, swings into holds and dismounts [1].
The rings event dates to the first modern Olympics in 1896, which Ioannis Mitropoulos won, and later champions include Jury Chechi in 1996 and Liu Yang in 2020 and 2024 [1].

Advanced calisthenics skills include front and back levers, handstands, L-sits, muscle-ups and the planche [2]. Statics are advanced isometric holds that include the front lever, planche, human flag and handstand [2]. Calisthenics also includes street workout competitions, which have been organised by bodies such as the World Street Workout & Calisthenics Federation [2].

In artistic gymnastics only the straddle and full planche are recognised; on rings the straddle is rated A and the full planche C, and each hold must last at least two seconds.[3] Practitioners reach them through a progression: frog stand, tuck planche, advanced tuck planche, straddle planche and full planche.[3]
Training logs on T Nation list ring support holds and pseudo-planche push-ups as part of upper-body sessions, alongside negative chin-ups and inverted rows.[6]

Snarr and Esco (2013) compared suspension push-ups with floor push-ups in 21 healthy adults. Suspension push-ups produced significantly higher EMG activity in the pectoralis major (69.5% vs 63.6% of maximal contraction), anterior deltoid (81.1% vs 58.9%) and triceps (105.8% vs 74.3%).[4] The study tested one suspension device, measured acute activity only and did not follow people through a training period.[4]

Wikipedia lists planche injury risks including torn ligaments or tendons in the arms, especially the distal biceps tendon, and injuries to the wrists, shoulders, elbows and back, as well as arm tendon inflammation.[3]

In a looksmax.org thread titled around gymnastic rings, the original poster describes ring workouts as engaging every muscle fibre and recommends them for people with some calisthenics experience. Replies say grip position in ring pull-ups is best, that ring dips lean toward strength gains more than muscle gains because of the stabilising demand, and that joints develop more slowly than muscle so rings let people add muscle while using joints less.[5]
No studies found of ring or planche training for appearance outcomes. The electromyography comparison of suspension and floor push-ups is the nearest published research.[4]

lore.intro: Ring and planche training is discussed in physique communities as a route to a gymnast look, mainly through short posts about enjoyment and muscle feel.[5]

claims.claim: Ring training activates every muscle fibre and is easier on shoulders and elbows
Ring dips build strength more than muscle because of the stabilising demand

timeline.event: Rings appear as an Olympic event; Ioannis Mitropoulos wins [1].
